title: Augustine's line helps us: without the written word we cannot know the apostolic point
source_text: XXI. Locus autem Augustini, quem pro se affert Bellarminus, mirifice pro nobis facit. Nam ibi dicit Augustinus quando hoc scriptum non est nos non posse id scire, cum Apostolum ipsi docentem non audiverimus. Unde manifestum est Augustinum non putasse quicquam certi posse haberi de Apostolorum praedicatione, ex traditione sola, sed tantum ex Scriptura sacra, quod certe nos volumus.
pass_a_gloss: But the place of Augustine which Bellarmine brings forward for himself wonderfully makes for us. For there Augustine says that when this is not written we cannot know it, since we ourselves have not heard the Apostle teaching. Whence it is manifest that Augustine did not think anything certain could be had concerning the preaching of the Apostles from tradition alone, but only from sacred Scripture, which is certainly what we want.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine's Augustine citation cuts his own way.
If it is not written, we who never heard Paul cannot know it.
So Augustine denies certain knowledge of apostolic preaching from tradition alone.
Certainty rests on sacred Scripture — our claim, not Rome's oral bank.

lemmas.latin: quando hoc scriptum non est nos non posse id scire
lemmas.gloss: when this is not written we cannot know it

choices.term: non putasse quicquam certi posse haberi ... ex traditione sola
choices.english: did not think anything certain could be had from tradition alone
rejected: Augustine endorses a parallel oral rule
